title: George Lewis's place in New Orleans jazz history
summary: Green divides history into original and revival periods and ranks George's influence.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: Um, how do you feel about George in relation to New Orleans jazz, uh, history let's say, and his position? And, um, how do you think people, uh, do you think you'll continue to be acknowledged or do you think you'll be considered greater when you get, when, as time goes on? Or do you think you'll be considered as long or, uh, do you have any sense of, uh, his position?

Yeah, I, I think, uh, you have to divide New Orleans jazz history into two periods. I think the original history and its death, its demise almost completely with your giant, with your Johnny Dodds and Ole Miss Simeon. And then, uh, nothing. And then the revival with George and Bonk. And then George Lewis emerging as really the, the great giant on the clarinet and maintaining this position. And the fact that this music ever got off the old scratchy 78s, I think, is in a large measure George's contribution. And the fact, no matter where in the world you go, kids playing clarinet are playing like him. They're not playing like Johnny Dodds. They're not playing like Ole Miss Simeon. They're playing like George Lewis. So in, in a sense, while I don't think you list him among the jazz greats of the early period, in many ways he proved to be greater and more durable than any of them. Mm-hmm. And his influence, I think, is stronger than Johnny Dodds, stronger than Jelly Roll Morton, uh, far stronger than a white musician, say, Beiderbeck. Uh, George Lewis lived and he happened now and he happened in our time and he ranked with the Giants. And now, when you go back and listen to the old records, you can fit George in and see what George, imagine what George would have done in, in these records and you realize how truly great he was.
